title: The System Design Interview
objectives: A 45-minute collaborative conversation where you clarify, estimate, sketch, and defend trade-offs.
Answer: What is graded in a design round?
Answer: First 5 minutes?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Interviewers grade how you think, not a single right diagram. They watch for: clarifying scope, sensible numbers, a clean high-level design, a deep dive into one hard part, and honest trade-offs.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: A 45-minute collaborative conversation where you clarify, estimate, sketch, and defend trade-offs.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Clarify requirements” to “Trade-offs & wrap-up”, via “Estimate scale”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Jumping straight into Kafka and microservices before asking what the product does. Spend roughly the first five minutes on requirements; the interviewer may steer you sooner.

cards.title: Worked example: the first five minutes
cards.body: Interviewer: “Design a URL shortener.” Good clarifying questions: Who creates links, and roughly how many per day? Do links expire? Custom aliases? Is click analytics in scope? A strong opening answer: “I’ll assume 100M new links a month, about 100 reads per write, redirects under 50 ms, links never expire, analytics out of scope. Let me size that before drawing anything.”

questions.prompt: What should you do in the first five minutes?
questions.explanation: Scope first. Every later decision depends on what the system must do and at what scale.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of a typical design interview.
questions.explanation: Requirements drive estimates, estimates drive design, and the deep dive validates it.

title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal + Load Balancers
objectives: Scale up with a bigger box or scale out with more boxes behind a load balancer.
Answer: Vertical scaling limit?
Answer: Prerequisite for horizontal scaling?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Vertical scaling is simple but hits a ceiling and is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling needs stateless services, a load balancer and partitioned data. It adds capacity, and it only adds availability if the copies fail independently and traffic is routed away from dead ones (health checks, no shared single database). Gains are rarely linear: shared state, coordination and hot keys eat into them.

title: OSI & TCP/IP
objectives: Place HTTP, TLS, TCP/UDP and IP in the right layer
Explain what a TCP handshake costs a request
Choose TCP or UDP for a given workload

cards.title: Why layers matter
cards.body: Interviewers rarely ask for all seven OSI layers. They ask which layer a component works at: an L4 load balancer sees IPs and ports, an L7 one sees HTTP paths and headers. Knowing the layer tells you what a box can and cannot do.

cards.title: The four layers you actually use
cards.body: Application (HTTP, gRPC, DNS) → Transport (TCP, UDP) → Internet (IP) → Link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). TCP gives ordered, reliable byte streams with retransmits; UDP gives fire-and-forget datagrams with no ordering.

cards.title: A new HTTPS connection
cards.body: 5 steps from “DNS lookup” to “Response”, via “TCP handshake (1 RTT)”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Ignoring round trips. From Mumbai to a us-east server one RTT is roughly 200 ms, so a cold HTTPS connection spends about 400 ms before the first byte. Keep-alive, connection pooling and edge termination exist to avoid paying that on every request.

questions.prompt: A live cricket score widget sends tiny updates every second; a lost update is fine because the next one replaces it. Which transport fits best?

choices.label: TCP, because every packet must arrive in order
UDP (or a UDP-based protocol like QUIC)

questions.explanation: Stale updates are worthless, so retransmitting them adds latency for nothing. UDP-based transports avoid head-of-line blocking. TCP would work, but it is not the best fit.

questions.prompt: Where does TLS sit in a typical HTTPS request?

choices.label: Between TCP and HTTP: it encrypts the byte stream TCP carries
Below IP, inside the network card

questions.explanation: TLS runs on top of TCP and below HTTP. QUIC (HTTP/3) folds transport and TLS together over UDP.

questions.prompt: Order what happens before the first byte of a brand-new HTTPS request.
questions.explanation: Name resolution, then the transport connection, then encryption, then the request itself.

flashcards.front: Which transport gives ordered, reliable delivery?
flashcards.back: TCP. UDP gives unordered datagrams with no retransmits.

flashcards.front: What does an L4 load balancer see?
flashcards.back: IP addresses and ports, not HTTP paths or headers.
Each new HTTPS connection pays TCP + TLS round trips before the first byte.

title: DNS
objectives: DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.
Answer: What does TTL control in DNS?
Answer: GeoDNS?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Browsers ask a recursive resolver, which walks root → .in/.com TLD → authoritative server and caches by TTL. Low TTLs allow fast failover; high TTLs reduce lookups.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.

cards.title: How a request flows

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Forgetting that DNS caching delays failover. A 24 h TTL means some users hit the dead region for a day.

choices.label: So clients pick up the new IP faster

questions.explanation: Cached records expire sooner, so the switch propagates quickly.

questions.prompt: Order a cold DNS lookup.
questions.explanation: Resolution walks down the hierarchy.

title: HTTP/HTTPS/TLS
objectives: Describe what TLS adds to HTTP
Count the round trips for a new HTTPS connection
Decide where to terminate TLS

cards.title: HTTPS in one sentence
cards.body: HTTPS is HTTP sent over a TLS-encrypted connection. TLS gives confidentiality (nobody can read it), integrity (nobody can change it unnoticed) and server authentication via a certificate chain.

cards.title: The handshake
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client hello (supported ciphers, key share)” to “Encrypted HTTP flows”, via “Server hello + certificate”.

cards.title: Where to terminate TLS
cards.body: Usually at the edge: a CDN or L7 load balancer decrypts, routes on the path, and talks to services over a private network (optionally re-encrypted with mTLS). Terminating close to the user cuts handshake latency.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Saying HTTPS makes an API secure. It protects data in transit only. You still need authentication, authorization, input validation and rate limiting.

questions.prompt: Your L7 load balancer must route /payments and /catalog to different services. Where should TLS terminate?

choices.label: At the load balancer (or edge), so it can read the HTTP path
Nowhere: send plain HTTP over the internet

questions.explanation: An L7 balancer can only route on paths it can read. Re-encrypt to services with mTLS if the internal network is not trusted.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HTTPS is accurate?

choices.label: It guarantees the server is fast
It removes the need for rate limiting
It protects data in transit but does not decide who may call your API

questions.explanation: Transport security and application security are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: A user in Chennai hits an origin in Singapore with about 60 ms RTT. Roughly how long before the first byte on a fresh TLS 1.3 connection (ignore DNS and server time)?

choices.label: About 120 ms: one RTT for TCP, one for TLS

questions.explanation: TCP handshake (1 RTT) + TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT) = about 2 × 60 ms before the request goes out.

flashcards.front: What three things does TLS provide?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.

flashcards.front: Why terminate TLS at the edge?
flashcards.back: Shorter handshakes for users, and the L7 balancer can route on HTTP paths.
No. It protects data in transit; you still need AuthN and AuthZ.

title: Containers & Kubernetes
objectives: Explain what a container packages
Describe what Kubernetes schedules and heals
Use readiness vs liveness probes correctly

cards.title: Containers package the process
cards.body: A container image bundles your app and its dependencies, so it runs the same on a laptop and in production. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in seconds rather than minutes like a VM.

cards.title: Kubernetes runs the fleet
cards.body: You declare the desired state (5 replicas of checkout, 512 MB each). Kubernetes schedules pods onto nodes, restarts crashed ones and replaces pods when a node dies.

cards.title: A rolling deploy
cards.body: 5 steps from “New image pushed” to “One old pod is removed, repeat”, via “Deployment creates a new pod”.
steps: One old pod is removed, repeat

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using the liveness probe to check the database. If the DB blips, every pod fails liveness and gets restarted at once. Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: The database is briefly unavailable and every pod restarts in a loop. Which probe is misconfigured?

choices.label: Liveness checks the database; it should only check the process itself

questions.explanation: Use readiness for dependencies: it stops traffic without killing pods.

questions.prompt: What does Kubernetes do when a node with 3 checkout pods dies?

choices.label: Schedules replacement pods on healthy nodes to restore the replica count
Moves the node’s disk to another rack

questions.explanation: Controllers reconcile actual state to the declared state.

questions.prompt: Order a rolling deploy step.
questions.explanation: Never remove old capacity before new pods are ready.

flashcards.back: Containers share the host kernel and start in seconds.
Failing it removes the pod from traffic without restarting it.
Failing it restarts the container.

title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
objectives: Contrast optimistic and pessimistic locking
Pick one based on contention
Implement version checks

cards.title: Two ways to stop lost updates
cards.body: Pessimistic locking takes a lock before reading (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Optimistic locking reads freely and checks a version at write time; if someone changed it, retry.

cards.title: Pick by contention
cards.body: Low contention (editing your own profile): optimistic, no waiting. High contention on one row (the last Tatkal seat): pessimistic or atomic updates, because optimistic retries would mostly fail.

cards.title: Optimistic update
cards.body: 4 steps from “Read row with version 7” to “0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry”, via “Compute new value”.
steps: 0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Holding a pessimistic lock while calling an external payment API. The lock lives for seconds and everything else queues behind it. Keep lock scopes short.

questions.prompt: Thousands of users race for the last 10 seats on one train at 10:00. Which approach suits the seat row?

choices.label: Pessimistic locking or an atomic conditional update

questions.explanation: Under heavy contention optimistic retries mostly fail and waste work.

questions.prompt: An optimistic UPDATE ... WHERE version = 7 changes 0 rows. What happened?

choices.label: Another writer changed the row first; re-read and retry or report a conflict

questions.explanation: 0 affected rows is the conflict signal.

questions.prompt: Users edit their own address once in a while. Which approach fits?

choices.label: Pessimistic locks held for the whole session

questions.explanation: Conflicts are rare, so avoid waiting on locks.

flashcards.front: How does optimistic locking detect conflicts?
flashcards.back: A version check in the UPDATE; 0 rows updated means retry.
High contention on the same rows.

flashcards.front: What should never happen inside a lock?
flashcards.back: Slow external calls like payment APIs.

title: OT vs CRDT
objectives: Explain why collaborative editing needs conflict resolution
Contrast OT and CRDTs
Know which needs a central server

cards.title: Concurrent edits collide
cards.body: Two people type into the same Google Doc paragraph at once. If each simply applies the other’s edit at the original position, their copies diverge.

cards.title: OT vs CRDT
cards.body: Operational Transformation rewrites incoming operations against concurrent ones, usually through a central server that orders them. CRDTs design data types whose merges always converge, so peers can sync in any order, even offline.

cards.title: Two users insert at once
cards.body: 4 steps from “A inserts “X” at position 5” to “Both copies converge”, via “B deletes position 2”.
steps: Server transforms A’s insert to position 4

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using last-write-wins on whole documents. One user’s entire edit disappears. Merge at the operation or character level.

questions.prompt: An app must let users edit notes offline on flights and merge later without a central server. Which fits better?

choices.label: Operational Transformation with a single ordering server

questions.explanation: CRDT merges are order-independent, which suits offline and peer-to-peer sync.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong with last-write-wins on the whole document?

choices.label: One person’s concurrent edits are silently lost

questions.explanation: Merging at operation level preserves both edits.

questions.prompt: Why does classic OT usually have a central server?

choices.label: Because OT cannot run in browsers
To give every operation a single order to transform against

questions.explanation: A single order makes transformation tractable.

flashcards.front: What does OT usually rely on?
flashcards.back: A central server that orders and transforms operations.
Replicas converge regardless of merge order, so offline sync works.
It silently discards concurrent edits.

title: Interview Playbook
objectives: Run a 45-minute interview in six stages
Ask clarifying questions before designing
Close with risks and next steps

cards.title: 45-minute map
cards.body: Spend ~5m clarifying, ~10m estimation, ~15m high-level design, ~10m deep dive, ~5m trade-offs and wrap-up.

cards.title: Drive the whiteboard

cards.title: Checklist flow

questions.explanation: Clarify first, size it, define the contract, sketch, go deep on one risk, then summarise.

questions.prompt: The interviewer says “Design BookMyShow.” What is the best first move?

choices.label: Ask which flows matter (browse, seat lock, payment) and the peak load, e.g. a big film release

questions.explanation: Scope and scale drive every later choice.

questions.prompt: Ten minutes are left and you are deep in one component. What should you do?

choices.label: Summarise the design, name the biggest risk and what you would do next
Start over with a new design

flashcards.front: What is the core interview takeaway for Interview Playbook?

flashcards.front: Which metric would you cite first for Interview Playbook?

title: URL Shortener
objectives: Scope URL Shortener: create short link from long url, redirect short link to original
Size it: 100M redirects/day, about 5,800/s at peak
Defend the design: generate ids with a counter/snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5t ids)

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 75 · URL Shortener: A bit.ly for SMS links sent by Indian banks and e-commerce apps. In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 75 non-functionals: Redirect p99 < 50 ms. 100:1 read/write. Links never collide.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 75 reference path: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids). → Store id → URL in a key-value store; cache hot links in Redis; 301/302 redirect. → Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 75 risks: Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links.

cards.title: Say aloud
cards.body: Boss 75 close: peak QPS for URL Shortener, required components client, lb, service, cache, nosql, and one mitigation.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in the first version of URL Shortener?

choices.label: Create short link from long URL

questions.explanation: In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry. Out of scope for this interview: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration; Video upload; Friend requests.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-functional requirement for URL Shortener?
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, durability and availability: Redirect p99 < 50 ms; 100:1 read/write; Links never collide. The others are features (functional) or out of scope.

questions.prompt: URL Shortener: assume 50M daily users each doing about 2 redirects a day, with traffic peaking at 5× the daily average. Estimate peak redirects per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 50M × 2 = 100M redirects/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 5,800/s.
questions.explanation: Average first, then apply the peak factor. 50M × 2 = 100M redirects/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 5,800/s. Anything within about 50% shows the right order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “Create short link from long URL” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Raise the client timeout so retries never happen
Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless
Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for URL Shortener jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does URL Shortener need for reliability?

choices.label: Keep user sessions in one server’s memory
Run a single database with no backups
Retry failed writes forever without idempotency
Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids).

questions.explanation: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids). Store id → URL in a key-value store; cache hot links in Redis; 301/302 redirect. Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links. The other options are common reliability mistakes.

questions.prompt: URL Shortener must create short link from long URL while side effects (notifications, analytics, indexing) also happen. How should the request be structured?

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

rationaleOptions.label: User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs
A queue removes the need to watch backlog
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request
A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.

flashcards.back: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry

flashcards.front: Peak load estimate for URL Shortener?
flashcards.back: 50M × 2 = 100M redirects/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 5,800/s.

flashcards.back: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids).

questions.prompt: Distributed KV Store: assume 10M daily users each doing about 50 operations a day, with traffic peaking at 3× the daily average. Estimate peak operations per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 10M × 50 = 500M operations/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 5,800/s on average; × 3 peak ≈ 17,000/s.
questions.explanation: Average first, then apply the peak factor. 10M × 50 = 500M operations/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 5,800/s on average; × 3 peak ≈ 17,000/s. Anything within about 50% shows the right order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “put(key, value)” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless
Raise the client timeout so retries never happen
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate
Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for Distributed KV Store jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does Distributed KV Store need for reliability?

choices.label: Keep user sessions in one server’s memory
Run a single database with no backups
Retry failed writes forever without idempotency
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes for partitioning.

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes for partitioning. Replication factor 3 with quorum reads/writes. Gossip membership, hinted handoff, read repair. The other options are common reliability mistakes.

questions.prompt: Distributed KV Store must put(key, value) while side effects (notifications, analytics, indexing) also happen. How should the request be structured?

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

rationaleOptions.label: A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request
A queue removes the need to watch backlog
User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.
